1 Pendubot technical guide

Current simulation dashboard notebooks and Python implementation

This guide explains the current pendubot project: define the robot, simulate its dynamics, calculate derivatives, optimize torques and feedback gains, execute the controller, and evaluate swing-up and stabilization. It covers full DDP, iLQR and local upright LQR together with the convergence dashboard, direct Python launchers and three executable Jupyter notebooks.

The saved benchmark shows that both methods converged to essentially the same objective and approximately 27 N m peak torque. Trajectory feedback passed the stated arrival and holding tests; open-loop replay was sensitive to integration differences and disturbances. These are results for the tested ideal model, not a guarantee for other parameter settings or hardware. [1-3]

Gravity9.81 m/s²

2 Coordinates and mechanical reasoning

Why the second joint moves without an elbow motor

q1 is measured from the downward vertical. q2 is measured from the extension of link 1, so the second link has absolute angle q1 + q2 and absolute angular velocity v1 + v2. The full link lengths are l1 and l2; lc1 and lc2 locate their centres of mass. The target [pi,0,0,0] points both links upward.

Centre-of-mass positions: horizontal X, upward Y

For uniform rods, lc1 = l1/2 and lc2 = l2/2. Replace lc2 by l2 to obtain the tip position. The browser canvas has downward-positive screen Y, so its drawing formulas use positive cosines; the physical coordinates above use upward-positive Y.

One motor and two joint coordinates

The motor acts between ground and link 1. It does no virtual work in the relative elbow coordinate, whose applied torque is zero. The elbow still accelerates through inertial coupling. At the default dimensions, the gravitational potential increases by 39.24 J from hanging to upright. The motor supplies mechanical power u v1; the cost term r u² is a squared-torque penalty, not an electrical-energy model.

3 Equations of motion

Derivation from the Lagrangian

Ii is the moment of inertia of link i about its centre of mass Ci. Define b = m2 l1 lc2, d = I2 + m2 lc2², and a = I1 + m1 lc1² + m2 l1² + d. Collect the acceleration, velocity-dependent and gravity terms to obtain the following model.

TermEntries in the chosen relative coordinates
M(q)M11 = a + 2b cos(q2); M12 = M21 = d + b cos(q2); M22 = d
c(q,v)c1 = -b sin(q2) (2v1v2 + v2²); c2 = b sin(q2) v1²
G(q)G1 = (m1 lc1 + m2 l1)g sin(q1) + m2 lc2 g sin(q1 + q2); G2 = m2 lc2 g sin(q1 + q2)

Default values and the state derivative

With m1 = m2 = 1 kg and l1 = l2 = 1 m, lc1 = lc2 = 0.5 m and I1 = I2 = 1/12 kg m². Thus M11 = 5/3 + cos(q2), M12 = 1/3 + 0.5 cos(q2), and M22 = 1/3. The gravity coefficients are 14.715 and 4.905. The minimum default mass-matrix determinant is 7/36, so it is nonsingular for every angle.

The code solves M times acceleration = applied torque minus c and G. Do not add the drawn weight arrows again: their generalized effects are already included in G. With zero torque and zero velocity, q1 and q2 in {0,pi} give the four resting equilibria and their periodic equivalents.

4 Deriving the base-joint equation

From an energy function to the first coupled equation of motion

The expression L = T - V defines the Lagrangian; the Euler-Lagrange equation supplies the mechanical law used to obtain motion. It follows from the principle of stationary action with applied generalized work. Here we use that law for each independent angle, with applied torques tau1 = u and tau2 = 0. The derivatives below show explicitly how the first joint equation is obtained.

1. Expand the energies in the two joint velocities

Write v1 = dq1/dt and v2 = dq2/dt. The absolute angular velocity of link 2 is v1 + v2. The constants a, b and d were defined on the preceding page from masses, lengths and inertias. Define alpha = (m1 lc1 + m2 l1)g and beta = m2 lc2 g. All these coefficients are constant for a fixed robot.

The mixed term v1 v2 expresses coupling between the links. In these coordinates the kinetic energy depends on q2, which changes the robot shape, but not on the overall orientation q1. Potential energy depends on both angles because gravity selects a vertical direction.

2. Differentiate with respect to v1 and then time

The extra velocity terms come from the product rule. For example, d(M11 v1)/dt = M11 dv1/dt + (dM11/dt)v1, and dM11/dt = -2b sin(q2) v2. Holding M fixed while differentiating would lose these terms.

3. Apply Euler-Lagrange with the motor torque

This is the base-joint equation: inertial terms plus velocity-dependent terms plus the gravity term equal the applied motor torque. Both joint accelerations appear because the two rigid links are dynamically coupled. The sign of G1 follows the chosen downward-zero angle convention and V = -alpha cos(q1) - beta cos(q1+q2).

5 Deriving the passive-elbow equation

The zero elbow torque still leaves a nonzero elbow acceleration

1. Differentiate with respect to v2

M22 = d is constant, while M12 changes with q2. Its time derivative contributes the last term. The derivative with respect to q2 must include both the kinetic and potential energies.

2. Subtract the q2 derivative and set tau2 = 0

Euler-Lagrange subtracts the entire expression above. The term -b sin(q2) v1 v2 from the time derivative cancels the +b sin(q2) v1 v2 produced by that subtraction. The remaining velocity term is +b sin(q2) v1², and the remaining gravity term is G2 = beta sin(q1+q2).

The right side is zero because there is no elbow motor. This does not impose ddq2 = 0: base acceleration, gravity and velocity coupling can all drive the passive joint. The two joint equations must therefore be solved together.

3. Collect the two equations into matrix form

M multiplies angular acceleration and contains inertia and coupling. The lower-case c is the already-multiplied vector of velocity-dependent generalized forces, not a matrix awaiting another velocity multiplication. G contains gravity generalized forces, with units of torque. The centres of mass C1 and C2 in the illustration are geometric points and are distinct from the lower-case vector c.

The code uses a symmetric mass matrix: M21 = M12. A single input u appears in the generalized-force vector, but inversion of the coupled mass matrix makes both accelerations depend on u. This is precisely the underactuated two-coordinate, one-motor system.

6 Constructing the continuous-time state model

Convert two second-order equations into four first-order equations

1. Choose positions and velocities as the state

A continuous-time state model gives the rate of change of every state at the current instant: dx/dt = f(x,u). Each second-order coordinate needs its position and velocity as state entries. The state has four components, although the applied input has only one component. The first two derivatives follow directly from the definitions.

2. Isolate accelerations using the mass matrix

Here r1 and r2 denote residual generalized forces for this derivation, not the scalar torque-penalty weight named r in Config. For this symmetric 2 by 2 matrix, the explicit linear solve gives the last two state derivatives:

3. Match the mathematics to dynamics(x,u,cfg)

dynamics first unpacks q1, q2, v1, v2; computes c and g; sets rhs = [u,0] - c - g; evaluates mass_matrix; and calculates det and acc with the formulas above. Its final concatenate returns [v1,v2,acc1,acc2]. The entries have units rad/s, rad/s, rad/s² and rad/s². No time step appears in this continuous-time function.

from pendubot import Config, dynamics
import jax.numpy as jnp

xdot = dynamics(jnp.zeros(4), 1.0, Config())
print(xdot)
# [0.0, 0.0, 1.71428571, -4.28571429]

At hanging rest, gravity and velocity terms vanish. A base torque of 1 N m still gives a nonzero elbow acceleration through M12. With zero input, both hanging and upright rest are equilibria. The example above uses the default masses and lengths.

The next section constructs the discrete map x[k+1] = F(x[k],u[k]) by integrating dx/dt = f(x,u) with RK4 over dt. The continuous model returns a derivative; RK4 returns a next state. For fixed parameters, f has no explicit time argument; time-varying control still enters through u(t).

7 Discretization and objective

The optimizer differentiates the discrete RK4 model

For one sample interval, hold u fixed. Fourth-order Runge-Kutta evaluates four continuous-time slopes. The symbols a1 through a4 below are integration slopes, unrelated to the DDP feedforward correction.

JAX differentiates this complete map F, including the intermediate RK4 states. The Euler approximation I + dt fx is not used as the derivative of this RK4 map. Fine execution uses ten substeps of dt/10, holding the same input throughout the original sample. This tests a finer numerical approximation of continuous dynamics, not an exact continuous-time solution.

Finite horizon cost

The running state weights reward approaching upright during the maneuver. The much larger terminal weights reward accurate arrival. The positive torque weight discourages excessive effort. These are numerical design choices, not uniquely optimal weights. Because state components have different units, the weights carry the scaling needed to combine their squared errors.

The duration is fixed at 6 s and the grid has 300 intervals. A soft terminal penalty does not enforce xN = xgoal as an equality constraint. There are no hard torque or state bounds. The optimization uses unwrapped errors relative to the specific target [pi,0,0,0], preserving the project cost. Only physical success metrics wrap angle errors modulo 2 pi.

Initial torque guesses

These are two starting points for a local optimizer. DDP and iLQR are run from the same sequence in each paired comparison. Neither method is guaranteed to find a global optimum.

8 The full DDP local model

The dynamics Hessian contractions distinguish DDP from iLQR

At each nominal stage, approximate the action-value function H(x,u) = g(x,u) + Vnext(F(x,u)). Let Vx and Vxx denote derivatives of the next-stage value at the nominal next state, A = Fx and B = Fu. Local deviations are dx and du.

The final sums arise from the chain rule applied to Vnext composed with nonlinear F. They contain the gradient of the future value multiplied by second derivatives of the dynamics. Full DDP retains them. The iLQR option removes these sums but keeps the terms built from A, B and Vxx. iLQR still rolls out the nonlinear dynamics during its forward pass.

Cost derivatives and terminal initialization

Tensor interpretation in the code

Pack z = [x,u], which has length five. Each output component Fi has a 5 by 5 Hessian. At one time step, fzz therefore has shape (4,5,5). Contracting its first axis against Vx produces a 5 by 5 curvature matrix, whose blocks supply the extra Hxx, Hux and Huu terms.

curvature = jnp.einsum('i,ijk->jk', vx, fzz)
# curvature[j,k] = sum_i vx[i] * fzz[i,j,k]
# state/state: [:4,:4], control/state: [4:,:4]
# control/control: [4,4]

9 Backward recursion and globalization

How the solver obtains a useful improving step

For a positive local control Hessian, the quadratic model can be minimized with respect to du. The code regularizes that scalar Hessian because the input dimension is one.

k is a scalar feedforward correction and K is a 1 by 4 feedback gain. Both are defined with the minus signs in the policy above. Alpha scales the feedforward correction during the forward line search; the feedback correction remains active along the candidate rollout.

Value derivative update

These expressions substitute the chosen regularized policy into the original unregularized quadratic model. They must not be replaced blindly by simplified identities that assume mu = 0. The Hessian is symmetrized after each update to reduce roundoff asymmetry.

Regularization and line search

The solve loop starts with mu = 1e-3. A backward pass is invalid if the regularized control Hessian is non-finite or at most 1e-10, or the updated value Hessian is non-finite. An invalid pass or an unsuccessful forward line search increases mu by a factor of ten. After an accepted step, mu is divided by three with a floor of 1e-9. At most sixteen regularization attempts are made per outer iteration; an excessive mu also stops the retry loop.

The candidate alpha values are 1, 1/2, 1/4, ..., 1/128. The solver accepts the first finite trajectory with a strictly lower true cost. It does not use a predicted-versus-actual improvement ratio or an Armijo condition. This is a simple monotonic line search.

Ordinary convergence requires both tests. A separate stationary status requires a small correction and no improving step at low regularization. The other statuses are iteration_limit and line_search_failed. Finally, the code recomputes feedback gains about the final accepted trajectory, rather than returning gains from a previous iterate.

10 Execution and upright LQR

Trajectory tracking and local stabilization serve different roles

During the planned maneuver

Open loop replays saved torque. Trajectory feedback adds a correction based on the current deviation from the nominal state. This is a sampled controller: the state is read and the torque computed once each 0.02 s. Ten integration substeps do not mean ten feedback updates.

After the planned maneuver

SciPy solves the discrete algebraic Riccati equation. QL = dt diag(100,100,10,10) and RL = dt times 0.1 in the benchmark. Scaling both weights by dt does not change the LQR gain. The interface lets you edit the scalar holding torque weight, while those holding state weights remain fixed. [5]

The saved benchmark gain is approximately [-146.0486, -133.4372, -61.5842, -33.0773]. Its sign follows u = -KL e and the chosen angle convention. The closed-loop discrete spectral radius is 0.946551, below one. This verifies stability of the local linearized sampled model, not a global nonlinear capture guarantee.

Success testNumerical requirement
Arrival at 6 sEach wrapped angle error < 0.05 rad; each speed < 0.10 rad/s
Additional 5 s holdEach wrapped angle error < 0.10 rad and each speed < 0.25 rad/s throughout, including the switch
Integration comparisonCoarse RK4 dt versus ten substeps with the same held input

A state norm combining radians and rad/s is also reported as a diagnostic. Because it mixes units, it is not the sole physical success criterion. An optimizer convergence flag is likewise different from the arrival and hold tests.

11 Model and derivative validation

Checks performed before interpreting optimized motion

model_checks in run_simulation.py checks physical consistency and the derivatives of the implemented discrete map. The following numbers are from the saved default benchmark. [3]

CheckMeasured resultMeaning
Equilibrium residual3.604e-15Maximum norm of f(x,0) over the four resting configurations
Mass matrix eigenvalue0.066279Smallest eigenvalue over 101 elbow angles; positive
Energy drift at dt2.050e-05 JMaximum absolute drift over 10 s
Energy drift at dt/102.859e-10 JRefining integration substantially reduces drift
Jacobian check6.214e-12Maximum absolute JAX versus central-difference discrepancy
Hessian check4.862e-10Maximum absolute discrepancy from finite differences of the Jacobian

What is actually tested

The passive energy test starts from [0.5,-0.3,0.2,-0.1] with u = 0. It compares mechanical energy against its initial value, using a 10 s run at dt and another at dt/10. The derivative checks use z = [0.4,-0.3,0.8,-0.4,0.5] and a central-difference perturbation of 1e-5. These are useful numerical consistency checks at stated samples, not exhaustive proofs over the whole state space.

The code asserts equilibrium residual below 1e-12, positive sampled mass-matrix eigenvalues, fine energy drift below 1e-6 J and smaller than coarse drift, Jacobian discrepancy below 1e-7, and Hessian discrepancy below 1e-6. Accepted optimization costs must decrease monotonically. Exact-model nominal replay is also checked against the planned trajectory with a maximum-error tolerance of 1e-8; the saved replay error is zero.

Why these checks matter

Wrong signs in gravity, an absolute-versus-relative angle error, or incorrect centre-of-mass inertias can still produce plausible moving animations. Energy and equilibrium checks test the physics independently of whether an optimizer reduces its cost. The Hessian test also checks the tensor-axis convention used by full DDP.

No new optimization benchmark was run to write this guide. The evidence tables use the existing saved experiments. The current source has been inspected to explain its actual behavior, including the distinction between the batch runner and the interface.

12 DDP and iLQR benchmark

Same dynamics objectives initial guesses and stopping criteria

Method and startObjectiveIterationsTime sPeak N m
DDP zero5.1753058576984.13226.969
ILQR zero5.1753058595940.95426.969
DDP sine5.1753058576213.48826.969
ILQR sine5.1753058594910.72626.969

All four trials satisfied the ordinary convergence test and the saved swing-up test. Terminal four-state error norms were approximately 1.87e-7. The small differences in objective and torque are numerical: no practical final-objective advantage of full DDP is demonstrated by this experiment.

For the zero start, DDP used 698 iterations and iLQR 594. For the sine start, DDP used 621 and iLQR 491. In these runs, iLQR was faster and required fewer iterations. Full DDP evaluates and uses additional dynamics curvature, which increases its work per iteration; the particular regularization and local optimization path also affect its convergence.

Timings exclude explicit shared kernel warmup and are single-run observations on this computer. They include derivative evaluation, iteration and final gain recomputation. They are not repeated statistical speed benchmarks. Do not generalize this ordering to other horizons, initial guesses or problems.

Unsuccessful short-budget attempts

At 300 accepted iterations, the objectives were 19.88846, 10.51551, 16.81151 and 10.48943 in the table order. None met both stopping tolerances. Those are unsuccessful convergence attempts with a restricted iteration budget; they are not evidence that the methods cannot swing up. Continuing the same deterministic runs resolved the convergence test.

13 Nominal state and torque histories

What the optimized motion does

The first-link angle increases from 0 to pi, while the relative elbow angle initially becomes negative before returning to zero. The passive elbow motion follows the mechanical coupling; there is no hidden second motor. The nominal base torque peaks near 26.97 N m. This trajectory approaches upright well before the 6 s terminal time and then uses small input to remain close to the unstable equilibrium.

A physically successful path should be judged from angles, velocities, input and the holding experiment together. A small final cost alone is insufficient. The plotted torque has no saturation. Adding a motor limit would change the feasible problem and may require a constrained optimizer or a different design, followed by renewed execution tests.

14 Disturbance and integration experiments

The same planned motion can behave differently in execution

Fine execution casePolicyAngle error at 6 sSpeed at 6 sArrival and hold
nominalOpen loop2.393e+009.653e+00Fail / Fail
nominalFeedback4.094e-081.657e-07Pass / Pass
initial offsetOpen loop1.932e+001.168e+01Fail / Fail
initial offsetFeedback4.005e-081.621e-07Pass / Pass
velocity kickOpen loop2.676e+006.398e+00Fail / Fail
velocity kickFeedback1.119e-054.370e-05Pass / Pass

Angle and speed columns are maximum absolute component errors, in rad and rad/s. The initial-offset case adds [0.03,-0.02,0,0] at t = 0. The separate kick case adds [0,0,0.15,-0.10] at t = 3 s. Both feedback cases passed the sampled arrival and additional-hold tests.

Exact-model, zero-disturbance open-loop replay succeeds. Under finer integration, small model-discretization differences grow near the unstable upright motion and open loop loses tracking. Applying local LQR at 6 s then starts outside its local capture region. The terminated traces and very large attempted torques in failed runs indicate failed recovery and numerical breakdown, not a useful motor requirement. No general disturbance bound or region of attraction has been established.

Python and JAX notation

The @ operator means matrix multiplication. ** means exponentiation. x[:4] selects state entries and z[4:] selects the one-element control slice. A transpose such as a.T exchanges matrix axes. np denotes NumPy; jnp denotes JAX NumPy. JAX functions are used inside differentiable computations, while ordinary NumPy is used for saved data and execution bookkeeping.

jax.jit compiles array computations; vmap applies a function across the trajectory stage axis. lax.scan implements the sequential time recursion inside a compiled computation. These tools accelerate evaluation but do not change the equations. The optimizer is not machine learning or a trained neural policy. [4]

16 The physics functions in pendubot py

Function by function explanation

Config and state constants

Config is a frozen dataclass: one object holds masses, lengths, gravity, sampling time, duration, weights and solver tolerances. Its n property rounds duration/dt. The interface separately requires exact divisibility before constructing it. GOAL and X0 fix the planned target and initial state. Changing an execution offset does not modify X0.

mass_matrix

This function accepts the two angles and a Config, computes the COM distances and inertias for uniform rods, and returns a symmetric 2 by 2 matrix. Only q2 appears in M because rotating the entire system without changing its shape does not change the inertial coupling in these coordinates.

dynamics

 51  def dynamics(x, u, cfg=Config()):
 52      q1, q2, v1, v2 = x
 53      b = cfg.m2 * cfg.l1 * cfg.l2 / 2
 54      c = jnp.array([-b*jnp.sin(q2)*(2*v1*v2 + v2*v2),
 55                     b*jnp.sin(q2)*v1*v1])
 56      g2 = cfg.m2 * cfg.gravity * cfg.l2/2 * jnp.sin(q1+q2)
 57      g = jnp.array([(cfg.m1*cfg.l1/2 + cfg.m2*cfg.l1)
 58                     *cfg.gravity*jnp.sin(q1) + g2, g2])

Unpacking x names the four state entries. The vector c contains velocity-coupling forces. g2 is the gravity term shared by both joints; the array g adds the first-link and second-link contributions. rhs later subtracts c and g from the actuator vector. The function solves the 2 by 2 mass system explicitly, then returns [v1,v2,ddq1,ddq2].

 59      rhs = jnp.array([jnp.ravel(jnp.asarray(u))[0], 0.0]) - c - g
 60      # Explicit 2x2 solve avoids an unnecessary general solver in higher AD.
 61      m = mass_matrix(x[:2], cfg)
 62      det = m[0, 0]*m[1, 1] - m[0, 1]*m[1, 0]
 63      acc = jnp.array([m[1, 1]*rhs[0]-m[0, 1]*rhs[1],
 64                       -m[1, 0]*rhs[0]+m[0, 0]*rhs[1]]) / det
 65      return jnp.concatenate((x[2:], acc))

ravel and [0] normalize a scalar or one-element input. det is the mass-matrix determinant. The explicit solve avoids a general-purpose linear solver inside repeated higher-order differentiation; it is algebraically the same as solving M acc = rhs. Concatenation places the velocity entries before the acceleration entries.

rk4 and energy

rk4 takes x, u and an integration interval, evaluates the four slopes, and returns the next state. It does not choose a control. energy computes 0.5 vᵀ M v plus gravitational potential and is used for physical validation. These functions share the same Config, preventing a separate animation model from determining the motion.

17 Solver setup rollout and cost

The compiled functions preserve the same model

 84      def __init__(self, cfg=Config()):
 85          self.cfg = cfg
 86          self.Q = jnp.diag(jnp.array(cfg.q, dtype=jnp.float64))
 87          self.QN = jnp.diag(jnp.array(cfg.q_terminal, dtype=jnp.float64))
 88          self.step = jax.jit(lambda x, u: rk4(x, u, cfg.dt, cfg))
 89          self.fine_step = jax.jit(lambda x, u: jax.lax.fori_loop(
 90              0, 10, lambda _, z: rk4(z, u, cfg.dt/10, cfg), x))
 91
 92          def packed(z):
 93              return rk4(z[:4], z[4:], cfg.dt, cfg)
 94          self.derivatives = jax.jit(jax.vmap(jax.jacfwd(packed)))
 95          self.hessians = jax.jit(jax.vmap(jax.jacfwd(jax.jacrev(packed))))

The diagonal cost matrices are explicitly floating point. This matters when browser inputs such as 2000 arrive as integer JSON values: a JAX scan requires its carried value Hessian to keep the same dtype throughout. The global x64 flag also requests double precision for tighter numerical tolerances.

step advances one sample. fine_step repeats RK4 ten times with one held torque. packed combines state and torque into one argument so both derivative orders can be computed with respect to all five variables. jacfwd returns first derivatives. jacfwd(jacrev(...)) gives the second derivative tensor. vmap batches stages; jit compiles the result. [4]

_rollout

101      def _rollout(self, u, x0=X0):
102          def body(x, uk):
103              xn = self.step(x, uk)
104              return xn, xn
105          _, xs = jax.lax.scan(body, x0, u)
106          return jnp.concatenate((x0[None, :], xs))
107
108      def _cost(self, x, u):
109          e = x - GOAL  # Deliberately unwrapped: exactly the specified quadratic cost.
110          return 0.5*self.cfg.dt*(jnp.einsum('ni,ij,nj->', e[:-1], self.Q, e[:-1])
111                                  + self.cfg.r*jnp.sum(u*u)) + 0.5*e[-1]@self.QN@e[-1]

scan carries the current state through the input sequence. Its collected output contains the successor states, so the function prepends x0 to obtain N+1 states. The cost function computes all running quadratic errors using einsum, adds the sum of squared torques, then adds the terminal penalty. The einsum sums both the stage axis and state axes, giving a single scalar objective.

warmup

Warmup evaluates rollout, derivatives, Hessians, backward pass, forward pass and cost once before timing optimization. block_until_ready waits for the compiled result. Without synchronization, a timing could measure queued work rather than completed work. A changed Config creates a new Solver and can trigger compilation again; the interface labels this stage separately.

18 Reading the backward pass

Map each code variable to the DDP equations

113      def _backward(self, x, u, jac, hess, mu):
114          # z=[x,u]; Hessian tensor axes are [output,z,z].
115          def body(carry, data):
116              vx, vxx, valid = carry
117              xi, ui, fz, fzz = data
118              a, b = fz[:, :4], fz[:, 4:]
119              lx = self.cfg.dt*self.Q@(xi-GOAL)
120              lu = self.cfg.dt*self.cfg.r*ui
121              hx, hu = lx+a.T@vx, lu+b.T@vx
122              curvature = jnp.einsum('i,ijk->jk', vx, fzz)
123              hxx = self.cfg.dt*self.Q + a.T@vxx@a + curvature[:4, :4]
124              hux = b.T@vxx@a + curvature[4:, :4]
125              huu = self.cfg.dt*self.cfg.r + (b.T@vxx@b)[0, 0] + curvature[4, 4]
126              regularized = huu + mu
127              ok = jnp.isfinite(regularized) & (regularized > 1e-10)
128              denom = jnp.where(ok, regularized, 1.0)
129              k, gain = hu/denom, hux/denom
130              # Substitute du=-k-K dx in the original (unregularized) local model.
131              nvx = hx - gain.T@hu - hux.T@k + (gain.T@k)*huu
132              nvxx = hxx - gain.T@hux - hux.T@gain + gain.T@gain*huu
133              nvxx = (nvxx+nvxx.T)/2
134              return (nvx, nvxx, valid & ok & jnp.all(jnp.isfinite(nvxx))), (k, gain)

The scan carry is (vx,vxx,valid): future value derivatives and a validity flag. Each data tuple provides one nominal stage. a and b are A = Fx and B = Fu; lx and lu are running-cost gradients. hx, hu, hxx, hux and huu are derivatives of H, not the user-selected cost-weight matrices Q and QN.

The einsum is the full-DDP curvature contraction. The iLQR branch supplies zero dynamics Hessians, so this same backward function becomes iLQR. regularized is a scalar because there is one input. Dividing hu and hux by it computes the policy correction and gain without a matrix inversion.

If the scalar Hessian is invalid, the safe denominator of 1.0 only prevents an immediate bad division. The validity flag still rejects the entire pass; those gains are not accepted as a valid control update. nvx and nvxx implement substitution of the regularized policy into the unregularized quadratic model. The reverse scan begins from terminal derivatives, moves from stage N-1 to 0, and returns stage-indexed arrays of k and K.

19 Reading the forward and solve functions

How an initial guess becomes an optimized policy

140      def _forward(self, x, u, ks, gains, alpha):
141          def body(xnew, data):
142              xb, ub, k, gain = data
143              unew = ub - alpha*k - gain@(xnew-xb)
144              xn = self.step(xnew, unew)
145              return xn, (xn, unew)
146          _, (xs, us) = jax.lax.scan(body, x[0], (x[:-1], u, ks, gains))
147          return jnp.concatenate((x[:1], xs)), us

_forward starts from the current nominal initial state. At each sample it combines the nominal control, scaled feedforward correction, and feedback on the candidate-state deviation. Because it rolls out nonlinear step at every stage, feedback affects all later candidate states. The result is an entire candidate state and input trajectory, not just a new terminal state.

solve

First, reshape the initial torque sequence to (N,1), roll it out and evaluate J. Reject a non-finite initial cost. Next, for each iteration, evaluate the derivatives along the current trajectory. DDP evaluates actual dynamics Hessians; iLQR substitutes zeros. Try a regularized backward pass and forward line search. If accepted, replace x and u, log the iteration, decrease regularization, and check convergence. An optional progress callback reports status to the interface without changing the optimization.

169              z = jnp.concatenate((x[:-1], u), axis=1)
170              jac = self.derivatives(z)
171              hess = self.hessians(z) if method == "ddp" else jnp.zeros((self.cfg.n, 4, 5, 5))
172              accepted = False
173              for retry in range(16):
174                  ks, gains, valid = self.backward(x, u, jac, hess, mu)

The final section evaluates the derivatives again on the final trajectory and computes its feedback gains. This matters because a last accepted forward rollout changes the nominal trajectory. Returning the previous backward pass would give gains about an older solution.

Returned fieldHow to use it
x, u, gainsNominal trajectory, input sequence and final feedback policy
cost and historyFinal objective and accepted-step convergence record
status and iterationsWhy optimization stopped and the number of accepted iterations
secondsWall time inside solve, after explicit caller warmup when used
gain_regularizationRegularization used to obtain the final stored gains

The solver returns a local solution even at iteration_limit. Always inspect the status and then execute the policy to assess physical success. Neither a successful line search nor a converged local optimizer enforces a hard arrival constraint.

20 Batch experiments and interface execution

Follow the same controller through two entry points

Reproducible batch runner

run_simulation.main constructs Config and Solver, runs model_checks, warms the JAX kernels, computes upright LQR, and solves DDP and iLQR from zero and sine guesses. It saves four plans, convergence CSVs, a comparison table, 300-iteration checkpoints and twelve execution combinations: two integrators, three disturbance cases and two swing-up policies.

make_lqr solves the upright discrete Riccati equation. execution applies open loop or trajectory feedback and then five seconds of local LQR. execution_metrics reports arrival and holding separately from optimizer status. plots, animation and make_report produce the reference evidence. The runner chooses the lowest-cost DDP candidate for execution; success is not used as a selection filter. Read that selection together with the success metrics.

Dashboard worker and result payload

interface.SCHEMA defines controls, defaults, units and ranges. validate checks values, time-grid alignment and kick timing. worker builds Config, warms kernels and calls Solver.solve for one method or both. Compare both uses the same initial control sequence. The lowest-cost result is selected for animation and passed to execute, which uses the editable execution offsets, kick, hold duration, integration fidelity and holding LQR torque weight.

Result fieldPurpose
settings / configValidated requested settings and numerical model configuration
comparison / selectedPer-method status, objective, iterations, runtime and selected plan
history[method]Accepted optimizer costs and step diagnostics for convergence
nominal_x / nominal_uPlanned swing-up states and torques
executionExecuted states, torques, LQR gain, success tests and error metrics

Local request-to-result flow

GET /api/schema supplies the form; GET /api/status reports progress; GET /api/result supplies completed data; POST /api/run starts a validated background job. A lock protects shared state, and only one optimization job runs at a time. The service binds to 127.0.0.1 and checks its served routes, Host header and run-request token. It is designed for local use.

Completed dashboard runs are stored under interface_runs/ as timestamped JSON and latest.json. load_example prefers latest.json when present; otherwise it loads the bundled DDP sine plan, fine feedback execution and DDP convergence CSV. The browser draws returned numerical data; it does not solve the dynamics itself.

21 The optimizer convergence dashboard

Objective versus accepted iteration is separate from motion playback

After a completed run, show(result) calls drawConvergence(). It builds one curve per method in comparison using history[method], converts values to numbers, discards missing or non-finite points, and sorts each curve by its own iteration index. The horizontal axis is accepted optimizer iteration; the vertical axis is objective J. Lower values are better for the stated cost.

What the scale and legend mean

The Objective scale selector switches between logarithmic and linear display. Logarithmic display is used only when every plotted objective is positive; otherwise the chart falls back to linear. The legend reports saved step count and final J for each curve. Changing scale redraws existing history and does not run an optimization.

Select Compare both, then Run simulation to obtain two curves from identical current settings and initial guesses. The chart updates after a run completes. Progress text can change during optimization, but the chart is not a live trace of an unfinished solve. Play, speed and the time slider affect motion playback only.

Missing history is not reconstructed

The bundled default example includes the DDP sine history. Older dashboard JSON files may contain no history or only one method. The chart displays an explicit missing-history message instead of inferring a curve from the final objective. Run Compare both again to generate both histories. A flat-looking segment is not proof of convergence: inspect status, relative cost reduction and feedforward correction as well.

22 Installing and reopening the simulation

Current Windows launchers invoke Python directly

Windows: double-click startup

Install Python 3.12 or newer. Run Install Pendubot.cmd once, then Launch Pendubot.cmd. Both CMD files select an existing environment Python when available, otherwise use py -3 or python, and call launcher.py directly. They no longer depend on running a PowerShell script, so the earlier scripts-disabled error is avoided without changing the Windows execution policy.

How launcher.py works

prepare_environment creates .venv when needed, checks JAX, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and Pillow, and installs requirements.txt if those imports fail. launch first probes the local health endpoint. A matching running app is reused. If a different application occupies the port, it reports the conflict rather than stopping that application. Otherwise start_server starts interface.py and wait_for_server waits for readiness before showing the URL.

Windows startup hides the helper process. Runtime output, errors and server PID are stored under .runtime/. Browser-opening failure still prints the usable URL. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ manually if needed. To use another port, run the following from the project folder:

python launcher.py --port 8766
python launcher.py --no-browser

Ubuntu or WSL: use a Linux environment

python3 -m venv .venv-linux
.venv-linux/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv-linux/bin/python interface.py

Run those commands in the cloned Pendubot_Opt_Control folder using Python 3.12 or newer. A Windows .venv cannot be reused as a Linux environment. In WSL, open the printed localhost URL in the Windows browser. A missing xdg-open or wslview only affects automatic browser opening; it is not a simulation failure. The CMD files are Windows-specific, while the Python service runs directly on supported platforms.

Troubleshooting by symptom

If startup fails, inspect .runtime/error.log for launcher-managed runs. If a port is occupied, choose another port or reconnect to the existing app. If model parameters change, JAX can compile again before optimizing. If optimization stops at iteration_limit, inspect its convergence history and increase the budget only when appropriate; reopening the browser does not improve the numerical result.

23 Changing parameters with a clear purpose

Dashboard changes rerun the plan; playback changes only its display

ControlMeaning and likely effect
m1 m2 l1 l2 gravityChanges the actual dynamics. COM and rod inertia are recalculated; regenerate the plan.
Horizon and sample intervalChanges maneuver time and resolution. More stages increase work. Horizon and hold must divide by dt.
Running angle weightsRewards approaching the desired angles during the maneuver; can alter swing strategy.
Running velocity weightsPenalizes speeds along the plan; very large values can inhibit fast energy transfer.
Terminal weightsPenalizes final error more strongly; larger values can worsen numerical conditioning.
Torque penalty rRewards lower squared motor effort. It does not cap torque.
Initial torque guessChanges the starting point of a local optimization; can change convergence or the local solution.
Feedback and integrationChanges execution policy or validation fidelity; does not redesign a torque-limited controller.
Initial offsets and velocity kickDisturbs execution, while planned X0 stays at zero. Kick time is rounded to the nearest sample.
Holding torque weightChanges local LQR effort tradeoff; holding state weights remain fixed.
Maximum iterations and tolerancesControls numerical effort and stopping; physical success is evaluated separately.

A controlled study

Begin with project defaults and save the run. Change one quantity at a time, such as r from 0.01 to 0.02. Record method, guess, cost, status, terminal error, peak executed torque and hold success. For a fair DDP-iLQR comparison, select Compare both before changing any other setting. Repeat timing trials if speed is a research conclusion; a single run is only descriptive.

A parameter edit marks the form as changed while the displayed animation and convergence chart still belong to the previous completed run. Click Run simulation to apply new settings. Reset restores form defaults and also requires a run to compute a new result. Save run data exports the currently completed result, including settings, comparisons, trajectories and histories.

Install support and open Jupyter

Saved outputs versus fresh execution

The delivered notebooks contain outputs from 35 executed code cells: 10 in Notebook 1, 13 in Notebook 2 and 12 in Notebook 3, with no cell errors. Notebook 2 performs new DDP and iLQR solves; its timings are distinct from the saved batch benchmark. Notebook 3 identifies saved reference files and then re-executes their plan for feedback tests. None of the notebooks overwrites results/ or starts the dashboard server.

25 Changing Config inside a notebook

Put replace immediately after the configuration is created

Config is a frozen dataclass: cfg.m2 = 1.5 is not the supported editing method. dataclasses.replace creates another configuration with specified fields changed. Assign that result back to cfg when you want subsequent cells to use it. Insert the following at the beginning of the parameter cell, before constructing Solver:

from dataclasses import replace
from pendubot import Config, Solver

cfg = Config()
cfg = replace(cfg, m2=1.5, r=0.02)

# Rebuild the model and optimizer with the changed configuration.
solver = Solver(cfg)

In Notebook 1, insert the replace line directly below cfg = Config() in Section 2. Then run that cell and all subsequent cells so the later Solver(cfg) receives the changed object. In Notebook 2, edit its own configuration cell, rebuild the solver and rerun the paired optimization. A change in Notebook 1 does not automatically carry into Notebook 2 or into the dashboard.

Why the order matters

Solver captures cfg in its compiled step, fine_step and derivative functions. Reassigning cfg after solver already exists does not change the solver. Construct a new Solver(cfg), regenerate the torque guess if N changed, warm the new kernels, optimize, and execute again. The Config.n property rounds duration/dt; choose exactly aligned time grids even when using a notebook without interface validation.

import numpy as np

t = np.arange(cfg.n) * cfg.dt
u0 = 4.0 * np.sin(np.pi * t)
solver.warmup()
result = solver.solve(u0, method="ddp")
print(result["status"], result["cost"])

Keep saved plans consistent with their model

Notebook 3 reconstructs Config from results/summary.json before loading a saved plan. Do not change its masses, horizon or planning weights and then assume that saved plan was designed for the new model. Use Notebook 2 to generate a new plan first. Its small dashboard-execution example changes offsets and kicks while retaining the saved planning model. The dashboard likewise plans from X0 = zero; execution offsets do not modify that planned initial state.

26 Verification and practical limits

Separate correct execution, convergence and physical success

Current regression coverage

Test moduleSix checks
test_interface.pyDefault settings; time alignment; kick timing; invalid/unknown values; integer iteration budget; integer terminal-weight backward-scan regression
test_launcher.pyReuse existing app; preserve other application on occupied port; use environment Python and wait for health; report startup failure; retain URL when browser opening fails; CMD files avoid PowerShell

The latest repository verification passed all 12 tests. Notebook verification separately executed 35 code cells successfully. Those checks support the stated implementation behavior. Source checks and document regeneration do not constitute a new optimization benchmark; the results on pages 11-14 remain the included reference experiments.

# Windows, from the project folder
.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest test_interface test_launcher -v
.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_simulation.py --output new_results

# Ubuntu / WSL: use the Linux environment interpreter
.venv-linux/bin/python -m unittest test_interface test_launcher -v
.venv-linux/bin/python run_simulation.py --output new_results

What the ideal simulation leaves out

The model assumes uniform rigid links, frictionless joints, exact state feedback and no torque saturation, delay or sensor noise. There is no collision model or hard terminal equality. DDP and iLQR are local optimizers. Fine integration and the tested disturbances provide finite numerical evidence, not a region-of-attraction certificate or global guarantee. Success checks occur at sample times, so intersample extrema are not certified.

The interface stops before storing a non-finite or excessively large new state; the batch runner pads failed executions with unavailable samples. The batch swing-success flag also requires the full execution to remain finite, whereas the interface evaluates arrival and holding separately. Very large failed-run LQR torques indicate applying a local controller outside its useful region and are not reliable motor-sizing data.

Reproducible reporting

Report settings, initial guess, method, stopping status, objective, terminal errors, peak nominal and executed torque, and holding success together. Compare methods from identical starts and weights. Keep failed or unconverged attempts in the record. Repeat timings if making a speed claim. requirements-lock.txt records the original saved Windows benchmark versions; requirements-notebooks.txt adds the separate notebook tools.
